Eastern school whiting (Sillago ciliata) is an economically important sand smelt inhabiting coastal waters of eastern Australia. Eggs of this species are demersal and adhesive, attaching to seagrass and other submerged substrates following broadcast spawning. Field surveys and laboratory rearing studies have provided detailed information on early life history, including the size and mass of recently fertilised ova. Based on the relationship between egg diameter and wet weight derived from congeneric species, the wet weight at birth is approximately 0.00015 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.00015 grams]. Hatching occurs relatively quickly, with yolk-sac larvae emerging after an incubation period of about 8 days [ab = about 8 days] when eggs are maintained at a temperature of 22.5 °C [T = 22.5 °C]. This rapid embryonic development is consistent with the warm-temperate spawning season of this species, during which water temperatures typically range from 20 to 24 °C and facilitate efficient yolk utilisation prior to the onset of exogenous feeding.

Upon yolk-sac resorption and the commencement of active feeding, larvae transition into a planktonic, exogenously feeding stage that persists for several weeks before metamorphosis and subsequent benthic settlement. Growth during this early pelagic larval phase is rapid under optimal thermal regimes. At a water temperature of 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C], the maximum reproductive rate of adult females is expressed through a combination of high fecundity and frequent spawning events. Spawning surveys indicate that gravid females produce approximately 380,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 380,000 eggs per spawning event], and given the protracted spawning season, individuals may spawn approximately once per day [F_R_i = spawn approximately once per day]. This high daily reproductive output reflects an iteroparous life-history strategy adapted to environments where larval survival is highly variable.

Sexual maturation in Sillago ciliata occurs at a moderate body size relative to the species' maximum recorded length. The fork length at puberty, at which point gonadal recrudescence and vitellogenesis commence, has been estimated at 22.5 centimeters [Lp = 22.5 centimeters]. This measurement is derived from macroscopic and histological examination of gonad condition across multiple populations distributed along the New South Wales coast. Alternative accounts, including those of Cleland (1947), have suggested a slightly higher value of 26 cm for the onset of maturity, possibly reflecting geographic variation or methodological differences in the assessment of reproductive readiness. The attainment of this size threshold typically occurs during the second year of life for most individuals, after which fish join the spawning stock and contribute to the annual reproductive output of the population.

The maximum recorded body size for Sillago ciliata provides an important reference point for understanding the species' growth potential and asymptotic length. The ultimate fork length, based on sampling of the largest individuals from commercial catches and research surveys, is 51 centimeters [Li = 51 centimeters]. Corresponding to this terminal length, the ultimate wet weight is approximately 1,400 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,400 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions fitted to a large dataset of individuals spanning the full size range of the species. This substantial somatic mass supports a reproductive output that is among the highest recorded within the genus Sillago. The strong positive allometry between length and weight underscores the importance of protecting larger, older individuals in the spawning stock to maintain the population's fecundity and recruitment potential.

Longevity is a key demographic parameter influencing the resilience of fished populations. Under the thermal conditions that prevail throughout much of the species' distribution, with a mean annual water temperature of 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C], the maximum lifespan of eastern school whiting is approximately 22 years [am = approximately 22 years]. This relatively extended lifespan for a teleost of this body size suggests a life-history strategy characterised by slow adult mortality and sustained reproductive output over many seasons. Age determination based on otolith increment counts confirms that individuals can persist for more than two decades, with the oldest recorded specimen reaching an age of 8,030 days [am = 8,030 days] at a temperature of 25.4 °C [T = 25.4 °C]. This longevity, combined with high fecundity and iteroparous spawning, renders the species moderately resilient to fishing pressure, although localised depletions have been documented in regions of intensive harvest.
